title: Gilroy Unified School District Building Future Ready Campuses, Renovation, Modernization Measure
summary: Measure M authorizes Gilroy Unified School District to issue up to $295,000,000 in general obligation bonds for facility modernization, safety and security upgrades, and classroom and career-technical construction across all 14 district campuses. It requires 55% approval, is projected to cost property owners an average of $59.14 per $100,000 of assessed value, and carries an estimated total repayment cost of about $623.3 million in principal and interest through fiscal year 2059-60.
what_it_really_means: The ballot label voters see is the standard California school-bond formula: improve education quality, modernize classrooms and restrooms, make safety upgrades, add career-technical classrooms, and replace roofs. The Complete Text of Measure M filed with the county, however, runs to several pages of essentially unlimited categories, covering every school building system: HVAC, plumbing, electrical, technology infrastructure, playgrounds, parking lots, security cameras, fencing, furniture, and 'all other costs and work necessary or incidental to the listed bond projects.' The Bond Project List authorizes this scope at all seven elementary schools (El Roble, Eliot, Glen View, Las Animas, Luigi Aprea, Rod Kelley, Rucker), all three middle schools (Brownell, Ascencion Solorsano, South Valley), and all four high school or other campuses (Christopher, Gilroy High, Mt. Madonna Continuation, Dr. T.J. Owens Gilroy Early College Academy) plus 'other support and related school facility sites.' No dollar figure is assigned to any individual project or campus anywhere in the measure text; the district retains full discretion over which projects get funded first and how much each receives.

The measure's own text states plainly that 'the order in which such projects appear on the Bond Project List is not an indication of priority for funding or completion' and that 'inclusion of a project on the Bond Project List is not a guarantee that the project will be completed.' Combined with the absence of any per-project dollar cap, this means a yes vote authorizes the district's Board of Education, not voters, to decide after the election which of the listed items actually get built with the $295 million, guided only by the district's separately adopted, non-binding Facilities Master Plan.

The $295 million is a fraction of what the district says it needs. Gilroy Unified's Facilities Master Plan, adopted alongside the decision to pursue this bond, identified roughly $700 million to $900 million in facility needs over a 10-year horizon (the district's own staff report put the figure at approximately $958 million). Measure M funds about 31 to 42 percent of that identified need, meaning most projects on the Bond Project List will compete for a pool far smaller than the list implies, and some will not be built at all under this authorization.

The Tax Rate Statement filed with the county, required under Elections Code Sections 9400-9405 and signed by Superintendent Anisha Munshi on May 28, 2026, gives three figures that the ballot label collapses into one: the average annual tax rate over the life of the bonds is estimated at $59.14 per $100,000 of assessed value (close to the ballot label's rounded '$59'); the highest single-year tax rate is estimated at $60.00 per $100,000, projected for fiscal year 2027-28, the first year bonds are expected to be sold; and the final fiscal year in which the tax is expected to be collected is 2059-60, meaning a homeowner who buys property in Gilroy today could still be paying down this bond in their retirement, 34 years from now.

The same Tax Rate Statement discloses the total cost of borrowing: 'the best estimate of the total debt service, including the principal and interest, that would be required to be repaid if all of the bonds are issued and sold is approximately $623,300,000.' That is more than double the $295 million in principal being authorized, meaning roughly $328 million of the total repayment is interest. This interest cost is standard for a 30-plus-year general obligation bond program and is disclosed exactly as state law requires, but it does not appear anywhere in the ballot question itself, which cites only the $295 million principal figure and the per-$100,000 tax rate.

Every one of these numbers is explicitly non-binding. The measure text states that 'the amount of money to be raised annually and the rate and duration of the tax to be levied for the bonds may vary from those presently estimated,' and the Tax Rate Statement repeats that the average rate, highest rate, final fiscal year, and total debt service 'may vary from those presently estimated for a variety of reasons,' including the timing and structure of individual bond sales and future assessed valuation. Voters are approving a $295 million borrowing authorization and a funding mechanism, not a fixed repayment schedule; the $59.14 and $623.3 million figures are the district's best current estimate, not a ceiling the district is legally bound to.

The measure contains a provision not evident from its title: if issuing all $295 million in authorized bonds would push the district's outstanding debt above its statutory bonding limit (2.50% of the district's total assessed taxable property value), the text states the district 'intends to seek a waiver of its bonding limit from the State Board of Education,' and that 'by approval of this measure, the voters have authorized the District to seek such a waiver.' No waiver has yet been sought or granted, but voters are pre-authorizing the district to ask a state body, not the local electorate, for permission to exceed a limit meant to cap local school debt relative to property values.

The measure also authorizes joint-use projects, letting the district partner with 'other public agencies or nonprofit organizations' and use bond proceeds to fund the local share of joint-use facilities eligible for state grants under Education Code Section 17077.42. This is standard in modern California school bonds but is not something a voter would infer from a ballot label about classrooms and roofs.

For any renovation, rehabilitation, or repair project, the district is explicitly authorized to instead demolish and build new construction if the Board 'determines that replacement new construction is more practical than renovation,' considering a building's age, condition, and comparative cost. A voter who reads the ballot label's promise to 'modernize' a building has, by approving the measure, also approved the district's discretion to tear it down and start over instead.

fiscal_impact.state_cost: none directly. The measure does not obligate the state, though the district states qualifying under this local bond may help it compete for state School Facility Program matching grants, which are a separate, discretionary state appropriation not guaranteed by this measure.
fiscal_impact.local_cost: Gilroy Unified School District property owners pay via an ad valorem property tax levy. The Tax Rate Statement estimates an average annual rate of $59.14 per $100,000 of assessed valuation over the life of the bonds, a peak rate of $60.00 per $100,000 in fiscal year 2027-28, and total debt service (principal plus interest) of approximately $623,300,000 if all authorized bonds are issued and sold, against $295,000,000 in principal.
fiscal_impact.revenue_change: Increases property tax revenue collected from Gilroy Unified School District parcels by an estimated $18,300,000 annually while bonds are outstanding, per district staff figures cited in local reporting; this is the local ad valorem levy needed to service the bonds, not a new general-purpose tax.
fiscal_impact.ongoing_vs_one_time: The $295 million bond authorization is issued in multiple series over time as the district needs project funds, not all at once. Repayment is a recurring annual property tax obligation on the district's tax rolls from the first bond sale (expected around fiscal year 2027-28) through the estimated final fiscal year of 2059-60, a period of roughly 33 years.
fiscal_impact.narrative: The measure text and the Tax Rate Statement are unusually direct that every headline number is an estimate, not a promise: the $59.14 average rate, the $60.00 peak rate, the 2059-60 final year, and the $623.3 million total debt service are all explicitly disclaimed as subject to change based on the timing of bond sales, market interest rates, the amount of bonds sold in each series, and actual future assessed valuation. What the ballot label's '$59 per $100,000' leaves out is that this is an average across more than three decades, not a flat annual amount; ratepayers will see the tax climb to roughly $60 per $100,000 in the first year of full collection (FY2027-28) and could see it move differently in later years depending on how the district times its bond sales and how the district's assessed valuation grows or shrinks. The gap between $295 million borrowed and $623.3 million repaid, more than double, is standard for a long-duration general obligation bond but is not visible anywhere in the ballot question voters mark.

new_taxes: An ad valorem property tax levy on all taxable property within Gilroy Unified School District boundaries, imposed to repay up to $295,000,000 in general obligation bonds. The Tax Rate Statement estimates an average annual rate of $59.14 and a peak rate of $60.00 per $100,000 of assessed valuation, continuing through an estimated final fiscal year of 2059-60.

new_spending_areas: Elementary school renovation, construction, and upgrade projects at all seven district elementary campuses: replacing portable classrooms with permanent structures, modernizing classrooms and restrooms, parking lot and access reconfiguration, Early Learning Center and Transitional Kindergarten facilities, energy-efficiency and HVAC upgrades, roof replacement, and physical-education facilities.
Middle school renovation, construction, and upgrade projects at all three district middle campuses, covering the same categories plus Career Technical Education classrooms and labs.

High school and other school facility renovation, construction, and upgrade projects at the district's four high school/other campuses and centralized operations and support sites, including gymnasiums, locker rooms, athletic fields, technology infrastructure, and safety and security systems (fencing, cameras, alarm and emergency communication systems).

District-wide technology, furniture, and equipment purchases and replacements, hazardous-materials remediation, seismic and code-compliance work, and joint-use facilities developed with other public agencies or nonprofit organizations.
Costs of the bond election and bond issuance itself, plus the state-mandated annual independent financial and performance audits, are explicitly counted as authorized project costs under the measure.
spending.funding_source: General obligation bonds secured by an ad valorem property tax on real property within Gilroy Unified School District, issued in multiple series over time up to the $295,000,000 authorized principal amount, requiring 55% voter approval under Proposition 39 (2000).

control_and_power: The Gilroy Unified School District Board of Education decides which Bond Project List items to fund and in what order; the measure text states explicitly that the listed order is not a priority ranking and that no project's completion is guaranteed. State law (California Education Code Section 15278 et seq.) requires the Board to form an independent citizens' oversight committee within 60 days of the Board certifying election results, with at least seven members drawn from specified categories: a business-community representative, a senior-citizens' organization representative, a taxpayers'-organization representative, a parent or guardian of an enrolled child, and a parent or guardian active in a parent-teacher organization, plus at least two further members. No district employee, official, vendor, contractor, or consultant may sit on the committee, and it may share members with oversight committees for the district's other bond measures (Measure P, 2008, and Measure E, 2016). The committee's statutory role is to confirm that bond proceeds are spent only on listed facilities projects and never on salaries or operating expenses, and to receive the results of the state-mandated annual independent financial and performance audits; it does not set project priorities, does not approve or reject individual expenditures before they are made, and has no authority to reallocate money between projects, which remains a Board decision. If issuing the full $295 million would exceed the district's statutory bonding limit (2.50% of assessed taxable property value), voter approval of this measure separately authorizes the district to seek a waiver of that limit from the California State Board of Education, a state body, without a further vote of Gilroy residents.
loopholes: The Bond Project List assigns no dollar amount to any individual project or campus, and the measure text states the listed order 'is not an indication of priority for funding or completion' and that inclusion on the list 'is not a guarantee that the project will be completed.' The Board of Education, not voters, decides after the election which projects are funded, in what order, and how much each receives.

Every headline financial figure (the $59.14 average tax rate, the $60.00 peak rate, the 2059-60 final collection year, and the $623.3 million total debt service) is explicitly non-binding under both the measure text and the Elections Code 9400-9405 Tax Rate Statement, which state these numbers 'may vary from those presently estimated' based on bond-sale timing, market interest rates, and future assessed valuation.

Approval of the measure separately authorizes the district to seek a waiver of its statutory bonding limit (2.50% of assessed valuation) from the State Board of Education if needed to issue the full $295 million, without requiring a further vote of district residents.

For any renovation, rehabilitation, or repair project, the district may substitute full demolition and new construction if the Board decides that is 'more practical,' a discretion embedded in the measure text rather than disclosed in the ballot label.

The Citizens' Bond Oversight Committee confirms spending complies with the project list categories and receives audit results, but has no authority to set spending priorities, approve individual expenditures in advance, or reallocate funds between projects; that decision-making stays with the Board.
unexpected_provisions: The measure authorizes the district to fund the local share of 'joint-use projects' developed in partnership with other public agencies or nonprofit organizations, eligible for separate state joint-use grant funding under Education Code Section 17077.42, a category not implied by the ballot label's focus on classrooms and safety.
Bond proceeds may fund the acquisition of real property, easements, rights-of-way, and interim storage or staging facilities needed for construction, in addition to renovating existing buildings.

If issuing all authorized bonds would exceed the district's statutory bonding limit, voter approval of this measure pre-authorizes the district to seek a waiver from the California State Board of Education, a mechanism embedded in the bond text rather than surfaced in the ballot question.

The total repayment cost disclosed in the Tax Rate Statement, approximately $623.3 million against $295 million borrowed, is more than double the principal amount cited in the ballot label, though the label itself states only the principal figure and the average tax rate.

The measure is structured as a single, indivisible ballot question under Education Code Section 15100: all of the enumerated purposes across all campuses and all project categories are voted on as one undifferentiated authorization, so a voter cannot approve, for example, safety upgrades while declining parking-lot reconfiguration or technology purchases.
pros: District staff argue the bond addresses critical, identified facility needs; the district's Facilities Master Plan found $700 million to $900 million in needs district-wide over the next decade, and Measure M is presented as a necessary, if partial, down payment funded locally rather than left to chance state funding.

The measure carries the accountability structure required of all Proposition 39 school bonds: mandatory annual independent financial and performance audits, a citizens' oversight committee, and an explicit prohibition on using proceeds for teacher or administrator salaries or other operating expenses, all written into the measure text itself.

The district's two prior bond programs, Measure P ($150 million, 2008) and Measure E ($170 million, 2016), were completed ahead of schedule and under budget according to the district's own public statements, which supporters cite as evidence the district manages bond proceeds responsibly.

A 55% vote threshold, rather than a two-thirds supermajority, applies because this is a Proposition 39 bond with the accountability safeguards (audits, oversight committee, no-salaries restriction) written into the measure, the standard tradeoff Proposition 39 (2000) established for California school facilities bonds.

Every campus in the district, from its oldest elementary schools (Glen View, first built 1953) to its newest high school (Christopher, opened 2009), is eligible for funding, meaning no single school community is excluded from the authorization even if funding priorities are decided later.
cons: The $295 million bond funds only a minority, roughly 31 to 42 percent, of the $700 million to $958 million in facility needs the district's own Facilities Master Plan identified, so many needs the district itself has flagged will remain unfunded after this bond is spent.

The true cost to property owners is more than double the borrowed amount: the district's own Tax Rate Statement estimates $623.3 million in total principal and interest against $295 million borrowed, a cost that does not appear in the ballot question voters will mark.
The tax is projected to run for roughly 33 years, through fiscal year 2059-60, committing property owners not yet born, or not yet living in Gilroy, to a tax obligation decided by today's electorate.

Residents commenting on the district's bond process publicly raised concerns about the district's declining enrollment and academic performance, citing reading proficiency around 55% and math proficiency around 19% districtwide, questioning whether a large new debt obligation is the district's most urgent priority.

The Bond Project List assigns no dollar figures to individual projects or schools and explicitly disclaims that its ordering reflects funding priority, so voters are authorizing a large sum without knowing which specific projects will actually be built or in what sequence.

The Silicon Valley Taxpayers Association opposes the measure and includes it among the November 2026 tax increase measures it recommends voting no on, consistent with the organization's historical opposition to prior Gilroy Unified bond measures.

The measure pre-authorizes the district to seek a waiver of its statutory bonding limit from the State Board of Education if needed to issue the full $295 million, a provision embedded in the bond text that voters approve without a separate, dedicated vote on that specific authority.

who_supports.notes: Voted unanimously at its May 28, 2026 meeting to place the measure on the ballot, following a Facilities Master Plan process and a commissioned voter survey.

who_supports.name: Dr. Anisha Munshi, Superintendent, Gilroy Unified School District
who_supports.notes: Signed the official Tax Rate Statement filed with Santa Clara County on May 28, 2026, certifying the district's cost estimates for the measure.

who_opposes.name: Silicon Valley Taxpayers Association
who_opposes.notes: Lists Measure M among the November 2026 local tax and bond measures it recommends a no vote on; the organization has historically filed opposition arguments against prior Gilroy Unified bond measures.
